BXL-2425-00031-v9.headline: Cut Brussels MPs' parliamentary indemnity by 5% on a permanent basis, applying the reduction not only to the base pay but also to the extra indemnities paid for special functions.
BXL-2425-00031-v9.proposed_by: Francis Dagrin, Oliver Rittweger de Moor, Francoise De Smedt, Jan Busselen (PTB/PVDA)
BXL-2425-00031-v9.source_brief:
On the table is a standalone proposal to reduce the indemnity Brussels regional MPs draw by 5% as a lasting measure, and to push that cut further than the parallel cross-party text by also shaving 5% off the top-up indemnities paid to members who hold special functions (such as Bureau seats).

- **What it changes:** a 5% reduction on the base parliamentary indemnity, framed as permanent rather than time-limited, plus the same 5% applied to special-function indemnities.
- **The money cited:** speakers describe a Brussels MP's net monthly pay as more than 7,000 euros, and special-function holders receiving roughly 2,500 euros extra.
- **The wider frame:** it lands amid a regional budget described as a 1.6 to 1.9 billion euro deficit, with cuts cited to associations (15%) and family allowances.
- **The rub:** whether elected members should cut their own pay deeply and permanently as a credibility signal, or whether a 5% trim risks underpaying the job and should align with other parliaments rather than go furthest.
deep_facts: The text is proposal for a decision A-103/1 - 2024/2025, tabled to reduce the indemnities of Brussels MPs by 5%; it was deposited before the parallel Bureau text and is described by its backers as going further (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

A competing text, A-150/1 - 2024/2025, was brought by the president on behalf of the Bureau, introducing a 'retenue temporaire de 5%' (temporary 5% retention) on the parliamentary indemnity from the first payment of the 2025-2026 session; the two were debated jointly but voted separately (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Backers of A-103 argued for two differences from the Bureau text: removing the 'temporary' character (making the cut lasting), and extending the 5% reduction to indemnities for special functions, not just the base indemnity (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
A Brussels MP's pay is described in debate as 'plus de 7.000 euros nets par mois', characterised by one speaker as making them 'les parlementaires les mieux payes de Belgique' (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Special-function indemnities are described as an extra figure of about '2.500 euros supplementaires' per holder; A-103's backers favour abolishing them and at minimum applying the 5% cut to them (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Backers note the Chamber of Representatives and the Flemish Parliament temporarily reduced their members' indemnity to 95% of the base salary of a 'conseiller d'Etat sans anciennete'; the Bureau text aligns Brussels on a 100% base, applying its 5% in that logic (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
Backers state that by renouncing their end-of-term departure indemnities in June 2024, their group allowed the Brussels Parliament to save 730.000 euros (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

The debate situates the measure within a regional deficit cited at '1,6 a 1,9 milliard d'euros' for 2025 and a consolidated debt that 'avoisinerait les 16,5 milliards d'euros'; cited parallel cuts include a 15% reduction in association budgets and the removal of a 10-euro top-up in family allowances for children born before 1 December 2019 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

A Bureau majority (cited as MR, Groen, Les Engages, Open Vld, N-VA) had a month earlier tabled a note to modernise the Parliament and cut its spending by 10%, bringing its budget to a figure cited at 62 million euros (from 57-59 million in 2024, having reached 14 twelfths / about 69 million in 2025 with provisional twelfths) (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Already-applied Bureau measures cited include scrapping the chauffeured car for the presidency, removing advantages for honorary MPs, ending staff provision for the outgoing president, and ending phone-cost reimbursement for Bureau members and group chairs (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
The PTB's longstanding stated position is to halve MPs' salaries; the 5% cut and the special-functions extension are presented as steps short of that demand (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Several groups (Ecolo, Team Fouad Ahidar, DeFI) voiced support for the substance of A-103 as more coherent or 'linear' than the Bureau text, since many members sit on neither the Bureau nor the enlarged Bureau; others (Groen) signalled they could abstain to respect the broader cross-party accord (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).

Tied debates flagged for future work: a 2014 rule change letting a single member form (and chair) a group with the attached costs; remunerating special functions on the basis of effective attendance; and a DeFI proposal to cut the number of MPs from 89 to 60 (CRI, 10 Jul 2025).
BXL-2425-00031-v9.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference - not stated verbatim in the record)*

- Two texts on the same 5% let members separate the gesture from its depth: backing the consensus Bureau cut while voting down the 'further' text lets a member claim the headline reduction without touching special-function pay or making it permanent.
- 'Temporary vs permanent' is the real wedge: a time-limited retention can quietly lapse, so insisting on permanence converts a symbolic signal into a structural pay change - which is precisely why it draws more resistance.
- Extending the cut to special-function indemnities reallocates pain toward members who hold Bureau and leadership seats, i.e. often the very people negotiating the Bureau consensus - a redistribution within the chamber, not just a cut.
- Framing pay against a billion-euro deficit and cuts to associations and family allowances builds an equity argument (the chamber should bleed before citizens do); opponents counter that an attractive indemnity keeps the mandate open to non-wealthy candidates and avoids a 'race to the bottom'.
- Voting against this text is not the same as opposing any cut, since a parallel consensus reduction exists - it can read instead as preferring alignment with other parliaments over going furthest.
BXL-2425-00031-v9.raw_fr: Proposition de decision A-103/1 - 2024/2025 visant a reduire les indemnites des parlementaires bruxellois de 5 %. Au-dela d'une baisse de 5 % de l'indemnite de base, le texte propose d'aller un cran plus loin en l'appliquant aussi aux indemnites pour fonctions speciales et en supprimant le caractere temporaire de la mesure. Les deux propositions (A-103 et celle du Bureau) ont fait l'objet d'une discussion conjointe mais d'un vote separe.
